title: Lecture 3: Introduction to Thermal Power Plants
section: 1. What Is a Thermal Power Plant?
text:
1. What Is a Thermal Power Plant?
A thermal power plant converts heat energy into electrical energy. The heat source may be combustion of fossil fuels, nuclear fission, concentrated solar, or geothermal energy. Regardless of the source, the working principle is the same: heat is used to produce high-pressure steam, which drives a turbine connected to a generator.
The majority of the world’s electricity is produced this way. Understanding how these plants work — and how to model them — is the foundation of this course.

Main Components







Component
Function




Boiler / Steam generator
Converts water to high-pressure steam


Turbine
Expands steam to produce shaft work


Condenser
Rejects heat, converts steam back to liquid


Feed pump
Returns condensate to boiler pressure


Generator
Converts shaft work to electricity

title: Lecture 3: Introduction to Thermal Power Plants
text:
2. The Ideal Rankine Cycle
The Rankine cycle is the theoretical model underpinning all steam power plants. It describes how a working fluid (water/steam) cycles through four thermodynamic processes.

The Four Processes
Process 1 → 2: Isentropic expansion (Turbine)
High-pressure superheated steam enters the turbine at state 1 and expands isentropically (no heat transfer, no irreversibilities) to the condenser pressure at state 2. Shaft work is produced.
Process 2 → 3: Isothermal condensation (Condenser)
Wet steam at state 2 rejects heat to the cooling medium at constant pressure until it becomes saturated liquid at state 3. No work is done.
Process 3 → 4: Isentropic compression (Pump)
The saturated liquid is pumped isentropically from condenser pressure back to boiler pressure. The pump work is small compared to turbine output.
Process 4 → 1: Isobaric heat addition (Boiler)
Compressed liquid is heated at constant pressure through the boiler until it reaches the desired turbine inlet conditions at state 1.


State Point Summary



State
Location
Phase




1
Turbine inlet
Superheated steam


2
Turbine exit / Condenser inlet
Wet steam


3
Condenser exit / Pump inlet
Saturated liquid


4
Pump exit / Boiler inlet
Compressed liquid

title: Lecture 3: Introduction to Thermal Power Plants
text:
3. Energy Analysis
For a steady-flow system, the first law of thermodynamics gives us the energy balance at each component.

Work and Heat per Unit Mass (kJ/kg)
\[w_{turbine} = h_1 - h_2\]
\[w_{pump} = h_4 - h_3\]
\[q_{boiler} = h_1 - h_4\]
\[q_{condenser} = h_2 - h_3\]


Net Work Output
\[w_{net} = w_{turbine} - w_{pump}\]


Thermal Efficiency
\[\eta_{th} = \frac{w_{net}}{q_{boiler}} = \frac{w_{turbine} - w_{pump}}{q_{boiler}}\]
Note that the pump work is typically less than 1% of the turbine output for steam cycles, which is why early approximations often ignored it. We will always include it in our calculations.

title: Lecture 3: Introduction to Thermal Power Plants
section: 4. Steam Properties and the IAPWS-IF97 Standard
text:
4. Steam Properties and the IAPWS-IF97 Standard
To evaluate enthalpies at each state point we need accurate steam property data. The International Association for the Properties of Water and Steam publishes the IF97 formulation, which is the industry standard for power plant calculations.
In this course we use the iapws Python library, which implements IF97.

from iapws import IAPWS97

# Superheated steam at turbine inlet: 500°C, 10 MPa
state1 = IAPWS97(T=500 + 273.15, P=10)

print(f"Temperature  : {state1.T - 273.15:.1f} °C")
print(f"Pressure     : {state1.P:.1f} MPa")
print(f"Enthalpy     : {state1.h:.2f} kJ/kg")
print(f"Entropy      : {state1.s:.4f} kJ/kg·K")
print(f"Specific vol : {state1.v:.4f} m³/kg")

Temperature  : 500.0 °C
Pressure     : 10.0 MPa
Enthalpy     : 3375.06 kJ/kg
Entropy      : 6.5993 kJ/kg·K
Specific vol : 0.0328 m³/kg


The IAPWS97 object accepts any two independent properties as arguments and returns all others. We will use temperature and pressure for the turbine inlet, and entropy for the isentropic processes.

title: Lecture 3: Introduction to Thermal Power Plants
text:
5. Baseline Cycle Calculation
Let us compute all four state points for a representative utility cycle:

Boiler: 500°C, 10 MPa
Condenser: 0.006 MPa (~36°C saturation temperature)


# State 1: Turbine inlet
state1 = IAPWS97(T=500 + 273.15, P=10)

# State 2: Turbine exit — isentropic (s2 = s1)
state2 = IAPWS97(P=0.006, s=state1.s)

# State 3: Pump inlet — saturated liquid
state3 = IAPWS97(P=0.006, x=0)

# State 4: Boiler inlet — isentropic pump (s4 = s3)
state4 = IAPWS97(P=10, s=state3.s)

# Energy balance
w_turbine = state1.h - state2.h
w_pump    = state4.h - state3.h
q_boiler  = state1.h - state4.h
w_net     = w_turbine - w_pump
eta       = w_net / q_boiler

print(f"{'State':<8} {'T (°C)':<10} {'P (MPa)':<10} {'h (kJ/kg)':<12} {'s (kJ/kg·K)'}")
print("-" * 55)
for label, state in [("1", state1), ("2", state2), ("3", state3), ("4", state4)]:
    print(f"{label:<8} {state.T - 273.15:<10.1f} {state.P:<10.3f} {state.h:<12.2f} {state.s:.4f}")

print(f"\nTurbine work   : {w_turbine:.2f} kJ/kg")
print(f"Pump work      : {w_pump:.2f} kJ/kg")
print(f"Net work       : {w_net:.2f} kJ/kg")
print(f"Boiler heat in : {q_boiler:.2f} kJ/kg")
print(f"Thermal eff.   : {eta:.1%}")

State    T (°C)     P (MPa)    h (kJ/kg)    s (kJ/kg·K)
-------------------------------------------------------
1        500.0      10.000     3375.06      6.5993
2        36.2       0.006      2031.62      6.5993
3        36.2       0.006      151.49       0.5209
4        36.4       10.000     161.53       0.5209

Turbine work   : 1343.44 kJ/kg
Pump work      : 10.04 kJ/kg
Net work       : 1333.41 kJ/kg
Boiler heat in : 3213.53 kJ/kg
Thermal eff.   : 41.5%

title: Lecture 3: Introduction to Thermal Power Plants
text:
6. Factors Affecting Efficiency
Three operating parameters have the greatest influence on cycle efficiency:
Boiler temperature — Higher turbine inlet temperature increases \(w_{turbine}\) without proportionally increasing \(q_{boiler}\), raising efficiency. Limited by material constraints (typically 600–620°C for modern steels).
Boiler pressure — Higher pressure raises the mean temperature of heat addition, improving efficiency. Limited by turbine exit steam quality — excessive moisture damages turbine blades.
Condenser pressure — Lower condenser pressure (lower condensing temperature) reduces heat rejection and increases \(w_{net}\). Limited by cooling water temperature and vacuum system capability.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def cycle_eta(T_boiler=500, P_boiler=10, P_condenser=0.006):
    s1 = IAPWS97(T=T_boiler + 273.15, P=P_boiler)
    s2 = IAPWS97(P=P_condenser, s=s1.s)
    s3 = IAPWS97(P=P_condenser, x=0)
    s4 = IAPWS97(P=P_boiler, s=s3.s)
    w_net = (s1.h - s2.h) - (s4.h - s3.h)
    q_in  = s1.h - s4.h
    return w_net / q_in * 100

temperatures = np.arange(300, 620, 10)
efficiencies = [cycle_eta(T_boiler=T) for T in temperatures]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.plot(temperatures, efficiencies, "ro-", linewidth=2, markersize=4)
ax.axvline(x=500, color="gray", linestyle="--", alpha=0.6, label="Baseline (500°C)")
ax.set_title("Effect of Boiler Temperature on Cycle Efficiency")
ax.set_xlabel("Boiler Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("Thermal Efficiency (%)")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Lecture 3: Introduction to Thermal Power Plants
text:
7. Steam Quality at Turbine Exit
Steam quality \(x\) represents the fraction of the mixture that is vapour:
\[x = \frac{m_{vapour}}{m_{total}} \quad (0 \leq x \leq 1)\]
At \(x = 0\) we have saturated liquid; at \(x = 1\) saturated vapour. Values below 0.88 are generally unacceptable in practice — liquid droplets erode turbine blades, reducing lifespan and efficiency.

print(f"Turbine exit quality (baseline): {state2.x:.3f}")

if state2.x < 0.88:
    print("WARNING: Quality below 0.88 — reheat cycle recommended")
else:
    print("Quality acceptable for direct expansion")

Turbine exit quality (baseline): 0.778
WARNING: Quality below 0.88 — reheat cycle recommended

title: Lecture 3: Introduction to Thermal Power Plants
text:
8. Looking Ahead
The ideal Rankine cycle is our starting point. Real plants deviate from this ideal due to:

Isentropic inefficiencies in turbines and pumps
Pressure drops in pipes and heat exchangers

Heat losses from the boiler
Feedwater heating stages

In subsequent lectures we will add these real-world effects and explore cycle modifications such as reheat, regeneration, and combined cycles that push efficiencies above 45%.

title: Lecture 3: Introduction to Thermal Power Plants
text:
Summary

A thermal power plant converts heat to electricity via a steam cycle
The ideal Rankine cycle has four processes: expansion, condensation, compression, and heat addition
Thermal efficiency is \(\eta = w_{net} / q_{boiler}\), typically 35–45% for modern steam plants
Steam properties are evaluated using the IAPWS-IF97 standard via iapws
Higher boiler temperature and pressure improve efficiency; low condenser pressure also helps

title: Lab 1: Boiler Efficiency Calculation
text:
Background
Boiler efficiency measures how effectively the boiler converts fuel energy into useful steam energy. Two methods are used in practice:
Direct method (input/output):
\[\eta = \frac{Q_{steam}}{Q_{fuel}} = \frac{\dot{m}_{steam} \times (h_{steam} - h_{fw})}{\dot{m}_{fuel} \times LHV}\]
Indirect method (loss method):
\[\eta = 1 - \frac{Q_{losses}}{Q_{fuel}}\]
The indirect method accounts for individual losses — the dominant one being stack (flue gas) heat loss. A complete indirect analysis also includes radiation, convection, and unburnt carbon losses.

Measurement Boundary
Feedwater (T02447, 254°C) → [BOILER SYSTEM] → HP Steam (T02602, 536°C)
                                    ↑
                          Fuel (G01038, 52.42 ton/h)
The economizer is inside the boiler boundary — its heat recovery is credited to the boiler in both methods.

title: Lab 1: Boiler Efficiency Calculation
text:
Setup

from iapws import IAPWS97
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: Lab 1: Boiler Efficiency Calculation
text:
Part 1: HFO Heating Value
Heavy fuel oil heating value depends on its elemental composition. The Dulong formula relates LHV to HHV:
\[LHV = HHV - 2442 \times (9H + W)\]
Where \(H\) is hydrogen mass fraction and \(W\) is moisture mass fraction. The factor \(9H\) accounts for water formed by hydrogen combustion; \(2442\) kJ/kg is the latent heat of water vapour at 25°C.

# HFO elemental composition (mass fractions) — X008xx tags
C = 84.0 / 100  # X00800 carbon
H = 13.4 / 100  # X00801 hydrogen
S = 0.6  / 100  # X00802 sulfur
O = 1.5  / 100  # X00803 oxygen
N = 0.5  / 100  # X00804 nitrogen
W = 1.0  / 100  # X00807 moisture

HHV = 41303.16  # kJ/kg  H00810

LHV = HHV - 2442 * (9 * H + W)

print(f"HHV              : {HHV:.2f} kJ/kg")
print(f"LHV (Dulong)     : {LHV:.2f} kJ/kg")
print(f"HHV - LHV        : {HHV - LHV:.2f} kJ/kg")

HHV              : 41303.16 kJ/kg
LHV (Dulong)     : 38333.69 kJ/kg
HHV - LHV        : 2969.47 kJ/kg

title: Lab 1: Boiler Efficiency Calculation
text:
Part 2: Direct Method
Using measured steam and feedwater enthalpies with actual fuel flow.

# Steam side measurements
h_steam = 3400.8    # kJ/kg  H02603  HP line steam enthalpy
h_fw    = 1097.1    # kJ/kg  H02448  economizer water inlet enthalpy
G_steam = 716.17 / 3.6  # kg/s  G02600  (ton/h → kg/s)

# Fuel side
G_fuel = 52.42 / 3.6    # kg/s  G01038  HFO supply flow (ton/h → kg/s)

# Heat flows
Q_steam = G_steam * (h_steam - h_fw)
Q_fuel  = G_fuel  * LHV

eta_direct = Q_steam / Q_fuel

print(f"Enthalpy rise    : {h_steam - h_fw:.2f} kJ/kg")
print(f"Heat to steam    : {Q_steam:.1f} kW")
print(f"Fuel heat input  : {Q_fuel:.1f} kW")
print(f"Boiler efficiency (direct): {eta_direct:.1%}")

title: Lab 1: Boiler Efficiency Calculation
text:
Part 3: Indirect Method — Stack Loss
The largest single boiler loss is heat carried away by flue gas. We calculate flue gas flow from fuel composition and excess air, then quantify the stack loss.

Step 1: Excess Air from O₂ Measurement
\[\lambda = \frac{21}{21 - O_{2}\%}\]

O2_fg  = 0.75   # vol%  X02419  O2 in flue gas (dry)
T_stack = 141.57  # °C  T02114  rotary air preheater gas outlet
T_ref   = 25.0    # °C  reference

lambda_excess = 21 / (21 - O2_fg)
excess_air_pct = (lambda_excess - 1) * 100

print(f"O2 in flue gas        : {O2_fg:.2f} vol%")
print(f"Excess air factor (λ) : {lambda_excess:.4f}")
print(f"Excess air            : {excess_air_pct:.1f}%")

O2 in flue gas        : 0.75 vol%
Excess air factor (λ) : 1.0370
Excess air            : 3.7%




Step 2: Flue Gas Flow

# Stoichiometric air requirement (Dulong)
air_stoich = (2.667 * C + 8 * (H - O / 8) + S) / 0.232
air_actual = air_stoich * lambda_excess

# Flue gas composition (kg/kg fuel)
fg_CO2     = 3.667 * C
fg_SO2     = 2.0 * S
fg_H2O     = 9.0 * H + W
fg_N2      = N + air_actual * 0.768
fg_O2_exc  = air_actual * 0.232 - (2.667 * C + 8 * (H - O / 8) + S)

G_fg_per_kg = fg_CO2 + fg_SO2 + fg_H2O + fg_N2 + fg_O2_exc
G_fluegas   = G_fuel * G_fg_per_kg

print(f"Stoichiometric air    : {air_stoich:.3f} kg/kg fuel")
print(f"Actual air            : {air_actual:.3f} kg/kg fuel")
print(f"Flue gas yield        : {G_fg_per_kg:.3f} kg/kg fuel")
print(f"Flue gas flow         : {G_fluegas:.2f} kg/s")

Stoichiometric air    : 14.238 kg/kg fuel
Actual air            : 14.766 kg/kg fuel
Flue gas yield        : 15.776 kg/kg fuel
Flue gas flow         : 229.71 kg/s




Step 3: Stack Heat Loss

Cp_fg = 1.10  # kJ/kg·K — approximate mean Cp for combustion products

Q_stack    = G_fluegas * Cp_fg * (T_stack - T_ref)
eta_indirect = (Q_fuel - Q_stack) / Q_fuel

print(f"Stack temperature     : {T_stack:.2f} °C")
print(f"Stack heat loss       : {Q_stack:.1f} kW")
print(f"Stack loss (% of LHV) : {Q_stack / Q_fuel * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"Boiler efficiency (indirect): {eta_indirect:.1%}")

Stack temperature     : 141.57 °C
Stack heat loss       : 29455.1 kW
Stack loss (% of LHV) : 5.3%
Boiler efficiency (indirect): 94.7%

title: Lab 1: Boiler Efficiency Calculation
text:
Part 4: Comparison and Sensitivity

print(f"Direct method   : {eta_direct:.1%}")
print(f"Indirect method : {eta_indirect:.1%}")
print(f"Difference      : {abs(eta_indirect - eta_direct) * 100:.1f} percentage points")

Direct method   : 82.1%
Indirect method : 94.7%
Difference      : 12.6 percentage points


The indirect method accounts only for stack loss. Observe how efficiency changes with stack temperature — a key operational parameter.

stack_temps = np.arange(100, 400, 10)
eta_stack = [(Q_fuel - G_fluegas * Cp_fg * (T - T_ref)) / Q_fuel * 100
             for T in stack_temps]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.plot(stack_temps, eta_stack, "ro-", linewidth=2, markersize=4)
ax.axvline(x=T_stack, color="gray", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7,
           label=f"Current stack temp ({T_stack}°C)")
ax.axhline(y=90, color="blue", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7,
           label="Typical nameplate (90%)")
ax.set_title("Effect of Stack Temperature on Boiler Efficiency")
ax.set_xlabel("Stack Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("Boiler Efficiency (%)")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Lab 3: Power Plant Efficiency
text:
Background
The ideal Rankine cycle is the theoretical basis for steam power generation. It consists of four processes:



Process
Device
Description




1 → 2
Turbine
Isentropic expansion


2 → 3
Condenser
Isothermal heat rejection


3 → 4
Pump
Isentropic compression


4 → 1
Boiler
Isobaric heat addition

title: Lab 3: Power Plant Efficiency
text:
Setup
Run the cell below to import the required libraries.

from iapws import IAPWS97
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: Lab 3: Power Plant Efficiency
text:
Part 1: Baseline Cycle
Run the simulation with default conditions:

Boiler: 500°C, 10 MPa

Condenser: 0.006 MPa (~36°C)


def rankine_cycle(T_boiler=500, P_boiler=10, P_condenser=0.006):
    """Ideal Rankine cycle using IAPWS-IF97 steam tables."""
    state1 = IAPWS97(T=T_boiler + 273.15, P=P_boiler)
    state2 = IAPWS97(P=P_condenser, s=state1.s)
    state3 = IAPWS97(P=P_condenser, x=0)
    state4 = IAPWS97(P=P_boiler, s=state3.s)

    w_turbine = state1.h - state2.h
    w_pump    = state4.h - state3.h
    q_boiler  = state1.h - state4.h
    w_net     = w_turbine - w_pump
    eta       = w_net / q_boiler

    return {
        "T_condenser_C":    round(state3.T - 273.15, 2),
        "h1": round(state1.h, 2),
        "h2": round(state2.h, 2),
        "h3": round(state3.h, 2),
        "h4": round(state4.h, 2),
        "w_turbine":        round(w_turbine, 2),
        "w_pump":           round(w_pump, 2),
        "w_net":            round(w_net, 2),
        "q_boiler":         round(q_boiler, 2),
        "eta":              round(eta, 4),
        "turbine_quality":  round(state2.x, 3) if state2.x else None,
    }

baseline = rankine_cycle()

print(f"Condenser temperature : {baseline['T_condenser_C']} °C")
print(f"h1 (turbine inlet)    : {baseline['h1']} kJ/kg")
print(f"h2 (turbine exit)     : {baseline['h2']} kJ/kg")
print(f"h3 (pump inlet)       : {baseline['h3']} kJ/kg")
print(f"h4 (boiler inlet)     : {baseline['h4']} kJ/kg")
print(f"Turbine work          : {baseline['w_turbine']} kJ/kg")
print(f"Pump work             : {baseline['w_pump']} kJ/kg")
print(f"Net work              : {baseline['w_net']} kJ/kg")
print(f"Boiler heat input     : {baseline['q_boiler']} kJ/kg")
print(f"Turbine exit quality  : {baseline['turbine_quality']}")

Serhat Beyenir is an instructor in Power Engineering at BCIT, where he teaches Thermal Power Plant Simulator courses and previously taught Thermodynamics, Applied Mechanics, Propulsion Engines, and Propulsion Plant Simulator courses at BCIT Marine Engineering.
His interest in computing dates back to high school, when he taught himself BASIC to plot trigonometric functions on an Amstrad 64K microcomputer. In February 2025, he attended a Python course at the West Vancouver Memorial Library and subsequently began using Python in his Marine and Power Engineering lecture materials, gradually incorporating computational examples into his teaching.

title: Lecture 1: Boiler Efficiency
text:
1. What Is Efficiency?
Efficiency is the ratio of useful output to energy input. It quantifies how well a system converts an input resource into a desired output, without waste.
\[\eta = \frac{\text{Useful output}}{\text{Energy input}}\]






Note



Efficiency and effectiveness are often used interchangeably in everyday language, but they mean different things in engineering:

Efficiency — minimising waste; doing things right
Effectiveness — maximising output; doing the right things

A boiler can be highly effective (producing large amounts of steam) while being inefficient (wasting significant amounts of fuel energy).

title: Lecture 1: Boiler Efficiency
text:
2. Boiler Efficiency — Two Definitions
Combustion efficiency measures the burner’s ability to completely burn fuel. It accounts for unburnt fuel and excess air in the exhaust. A burner with high combustion efficiency releases nearly all the chemical energy available in the fuel.
Thermal efficiency measures the heat exchanger’s ability to transfer heat from the combustion gases to the water and steam. Even with perfect combustion, heat can be lost through the stack, radiation from boiler surfaces, and blowdown.
In practice, boiler thermal efficiency is the combined result of both processes and is the primary performance indicator used in power plant operations:
\[\eta_{\text{boiler}} = \frac{\text{Energy transferred to steam}}{\text{Energy released by fuel}}\]

title: Lecture 1: Boiler Efficiency
text:
3. Boiler Thermal Efficiency — Direct Method
The direct (input/output) method computes efficiency from measured steam and fuel quantities. Let:

\(\dot{m}_s\) = steam mass flow rate (kg/s)
\(h_2\) = specific enthalpy of steam at boiler outlet (kJ/kg)
\(h_1\) = specific enthalpy of feedwater at boiler inlet (kJ/kg)
\(\dot{m}_f\) = fuel mass flow rate (kg/s)
\(HV\) = heating value of fuel (kJ/kg)

Since steam is generated at constant pressure, the heat absorbed per kg of steam is \((h_2 - h_1)\). The boiler thermal efficiency is therefore:
\[\eta_{\text{boiler}} = \frac{\dot{m}_s (h_2 - h_1)}{\dot{m}_f \times HV} \times 100\%\]

Measurement Boundary
The boundary defines what is included in the calculation. For a complete boiler system:
Feedwater inlet (h₁) → [Economizer → Steam drum → Superheater] → Steam outlet (h₂)
                                         ↑
                               Fuel input (ṁ_f × HV)
The economizer is inside the boundary — its heat recovery is credited to the boiler. The feedwater enthalpy \(h_1\) is measured at the economizer water inlet, not at the feedpump outlet.

title: Lecture 1: Boiler Efficiency
text:
4. Fuel Heating Values

Higher and Lower Heating Value
Fuel contains hydrogen which, on combustion, produces water vapour. The Higher Heating Value (HHV) assumes this water condenses and its latent heat is recovered. The Lower Heating Value (LHV) assumes water remains as vapour and the latent heat is lost with the flue gas.
Boiler efficiency in marine and power engineering is always quoted on the LHV basis because the flue gas exits above the dew point and the latent heat is not recovered in practice.


Dulong Formula
LHV can be calculated from elemental composition:
\[LHV = HHV - 2442 \times (9H + W)\]
Where:

\(H\) = hydrogen mass fraction
\(W\) = moisture mass fraction
\(2442\) kJ/kg = latent heat of water vapour at 25°C
\(9H\) = mass of water formed per kg fuel from hydrogen combustion


# HFO elemental composition (mass fractions) — X008xx tags
C = 84.0 / 100   # X00800 carbon
H = 13.4 / 100   # X00801 hydrogen
S = 0.6  / 100   # X00802 sulfur
O_frac = 1.5 / 100  # X00803 oxygen
N = 0.5  / 100   # X00804 nitrogen
W = 1.0  / 100   # X00807 moisture

HHV = 41303.16   # kJ/kg  H00810

LHV = HHV - 2442 * (9 * H + W)

print(f"LHV (Dulong)     : {LHV:.2f} kJ/kg")

5. Steam Properties and Enthalpy
Accurate enthalpy values are essential for boiler efficiency calculations. We use the IAPWS-IF97 standard via the iapws library.

from iapws import IAPWS97

# Boiler operating conditions from simulator
P_steam = 158.48 * 0.1       # bara → MPa
T_steam = 535.85 + 273.15    # °C → K
P_fw    = 201.97 * 0.1       # bara → MPa
T_fw    = 254.47 + 273.15    # °C → K

steam    = IAPWS97(T=T_steam, P=P_steam)
feedwater = IAPWS97(T=T_fw,   P=P_fw)

print(f"HP steam:")
print(f"  Temperature : {steam.T - 273.15:.2f} °C")

title: Lecture 1: Boiler Efficiency
text:
7. Factors Affecting Boiler Efficiency

Fuel Type
Different fuels have different hydrogen content, moisture, and ash levels, all of which affect the HHV/LHV gap and combustion behaviour.



Fuel
Typical LHV (kJ/kg)
H content
Notes




HFO
38,000–40,500
~13%
High H → large HHV/LHV gap


Coal
24,000–30,000
~5%
High ash, soot fouling


Biofuel (pellets)
17,000–19,000
~6%
High moisture


Natural gas
47,000–50,000
~25%
Cleanest combustion





Boiler Load
Boiler efficiency is not constant across the load range. At part load:

Fixed losses (radiation, convection) become a larger fraction of fuel input
Excess air tends to increase, raising stack losses
Heat transfer surfaces may be oversized, altering flue gas temperatures



Soot Fouling
Soot deposits on heat transfer surfaces act as insulation, reducing heat transfer from flue gas to steam. This raises flue gas outlet temperature and stack losses, directly reducing efficiency.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Illustrative efficiency vs load curve
load = np.array([30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100])
eta_clean = np.array([78, 80, 81, 82, 82.5, 82.1, 81.5, 80.5])
eta_soot  = np.array([74, 76, 77, 78, 78.5, 78.0, 77.5, 76.5])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.plot(load, eta_clean, "bo-", linewidth=2, markersize=6, label="Clean surfaces")
ax.plot(load, eta_soot,  "ro--", linewidth=2, markersize=6, label="Soot fouling")
ax.fill_between(load, eta_soot, eta_clean, alpha=0.15, color="gray",
                label="Efficiency penalty")
ax.set_title("Boiler Efficiency vs Load — Effect of Soot Fouling")
ax.set_xlabel("Boiler Load (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("Thermal Efficiency (%)")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Lecture 1: Boiler Efficiency
text:
9. Summary

Boiler thermal efficiency = energy to steam / energy from fuel
Always use LHV as the fuel energy basis
LHV is calculated from HHV using the Dulong formula
Accurate enthalpy values require steam tables (IAPWS-IF97)
Efficiency is influenced by fuel type, load, and surface cleanliness
In Lab 1 you will calculate efficiency for four conditions: HFO at 230 MW, biofuel at 80%, coal at 80%, and coal with soot
